title: Thalamic Morphology Modulates Thalamocortical Coupling in Insomnia
summary: This hypothesis proposes that thalamic morphology influences thalamocortical coupling in insomnia, linking structural and functional brain changes.
content: Thalamic morphology modulates thalamocortical coupling in insomnia, such that structural changes in the thalamus alter the functional connectivity between the thalamus and the default mode network (DMN), contributing to insomnia symptoms.
rationale: Evidence from the knowledge graph shows that thalamic morphology is associated with thalamus volume (E12), and thalamocortical coupling is linked to thalamus-DMN functional connectivity (E1-E3). Structural changes in the thalamus could thus influence the functional connectivity patterns observed in insomnia.
experimental_plan: Use MRI to measure thalamic volume and fMRI to assess thalamus-DMN functional connectivity in insomnia patients. Compare these measures with control subjects and correlate thalamic volume with thalamus-DMN FC.
novelty_assessment: This hypothesis integrates structural and functional neuroimaging data, linking thalamic morphology with thalamocortical coupling, which has not been explicitly tested in prior hypotheses.
key_assumptions: Thalamic volume is a measurable structural marker of thalamic morphology.
Thalamus-DMN functional connectivity is a reliable measure of thalamocortical coupling.

metadata.directional_prediction: Increased thalamic volume correlates with altered thalamus-DMN FC in insomnia patients compared to controls.
metadata.falsification_criteria: No significant correlation between thalamic volume and thalamus-DMN FC in insomnia patients compared to controls.

title: Thalamocortical Coupling Modulates Insomnia Severity via Structural Morphology and White Matter Integrity
summary: This hypothesis proposes that thalamocortical coupling modulates insomnia severity through a dual pathway involving structural morphology and white matter integrity, integrating multimodal neuroimaging data.
content: Thalamocortical coupling modulates insomnia severity through a dual pathway involving structural morphology of the thalamus and white matter integrity, as measured by MRI and DTI, respectively. This pathway integrates both functional and structural neuroimaging data to explain the neurobiological basis of insomnia severity.
rationale: The evidence supports a strong link between thalamocortical coupling and thalamus_DMN_FC (E1, E2, E3), as well as between structural morphology and MRI (E4, E12) and white matter integrity and FA (E10, E11). These findings suggest a potential interaction between thalamocortical coupling, structural morphology, and white matter integrity in modulating insomnia severity.
experimental_plan: Conduct a multimodal neuroimaging study combining EEG-fMRI, MRI, and DTI in a cohort of insomnia patients. Measure thalamocortical coupling (thalamus_DMN_FC), structural morphology (MRI), and white matter integrity (FA). Use regression models to assess the relationship between thalamocortical coupling and insomnia severity, mediated by structural morphology and white matter integrity.
novelty_assessment: This hypothesis introduces a dual pathway involving both structural morphology and white matter integrity, which has not been previously integrated in the context of thalamocortical coupling and insomnia severity.
key_assumptions: Thalamocortical coupling is modulated by structural morphology of the thalamus.
White matter integrity mediates the relationship between thalamocortical coupling and insomnia severity.

metadata.directional_prediction: Higher thalamocortical coupling is associated with higher insomnia severity, mediated by reduced structural morphology and reduced white matter integrity.
metadata.falsification_criteria: If thalamocortical coupling is not significantly associated with insomnia severity after controlling for structural morphology and white matter integrity, the hypothesis is refuted.
knowledge_graph_paths: white matter integrity -> FA -> insomnia severity

title: Thalamic Morphology Modulates Thalamocortical Coupling via White Matter Integrity in Insomnia
summary: This hypothesis proposes that thalamic morphology influences thalamocortical coupling through white matter integrity in insomnia, integrating structural and functional neuroimaging data.
content: Thalamic morphology modulates thalamocortical coupling in insomnia through the mediation of white matter integrity, linking structural, white matter, and functional brain changes.
rationale: Evidence shows thalamic morphology is related to thalamus volume (E12), white matter integrity is linked to FA (E10), and thalamocortical coupling is associated with thalamus_DMN_FC (E1). The integration of these pathways suggests a mediated relationship through white matter integrity.
experimental_plan: Use DTI to measure white matter integrity (FA) and fMRI to assess thalamocortical coupling (thalamus_DMN_FC) in insomnia patients with varying thalamic volumes.
novelty_assessment: Novel integration of thalamic morphology, white matter integrity, and thalamocortical coupling in insomnia, avoiding prior hypotheses that focused on direct structural-functional links without white matter mediation.
key_assumptions: Thalamic morphology affects white matter integrity
White matter integrity mediates thalamocortical coupling

metadata.neural_mechanism: thalamic morphology modulating thalamocortical coupling via white matter integrity
metadata.directional_prediction: Higher thalamic volume correlates with higher FA and stronger thalamocortical coupling in insomnia patients.
metadata.falsification_criteria: No correlation between thalamic volume and FA or thalamocortical coupling in insomnia patients.

title: Thalamic Morphology Mediates Thalamocortical Coupling via White Matter Integrity in Insomnia
summary: This hypothesis integrates thalamic morphology, white matter integrity, and thalamocortical coupling to explain insomnia severity, combining structural and functional pathways.
content: Thalamic morphology modulates thalamocortical coupling in insomnia through white matter integrity, integrating structural MRI, DTI, and fMRI data to show a mediated pathway from thalamic volume to insomnia severity via fractional anisotropy (FA) and thalamus-DMN functional connectivity.
rationale: Cross-pollination strengthens the integration of structural and functional pathways by incorporating white matter integrity as a mediator, improving coherence between P1, P2, and P3.
experimental_plan: Use MRI to measure thalamic volume, DTI to assess FA, and fMRI to measure thalamus-DMN FC in insomnia patients. Apply mediation analysis to test the pathway thalamic volume -> FA -> thalamus-DMN FC -> insomnia severity.
novelty_assessment: Enhances P3 by explicitly testing the mediation of white matter integrity, and integrates P2's thalamic morphology focus with P1's multimodal approach.
